result.topic_en: Euler takes the series for the arc Φ in terms of sines of multiples of Φ, specialises it to n = 1 − m, and differentiates and sets Φ = 0 to obtain the series 1/m − 1/(1−m) + 1/(1+m) − … = π cos mπ / sin mπ, giving a relation between integrals of the form ∫x^{m−1}dx(1−x)^{k}.
result.transcription:
178
$a = m\Phi;\ b = n\Phi;\ c = (1+m)\Phi;$
$d = (1+n)\Phi;\ e = (2+m)\Phi;\ f = (2+n)\Phi;$ etc.
ex eorum finibus longitudinem arcus $\Phi$ definire.
Solutio generalis supra data (7) suppeditat hanc aequationem:
$\Phi = \frac{\sin.m\Phi}{m}\cdot\frac{n\,n}{(n-m)(n+m)}\cdot\ldots$ etc. [?]
$-\frac{\sin.n\Phi}{n}\cdot\frac{m\,m}{(m-n)(m+n)}\cdot\ldots$ etc. [?]
$+\frac{\sin.(1+m)\Phi}{1+m}\cdot\ldots$ etc. [?]
$-\frac{\sin.(1+n)\Phi}{1+n}\cdot\ldots$ etc. [?]
$+\frac{\sin.(2+m)\Phi}{2+m}\cdot\ldots$ etc. [?]
etc.
Hinc autem in genere nihil attentione dignum concludere licet, vnde casum praecipue memorabilem euoluam, quo est $n = 1 - m$, pro quo statuo breuitatis gratia:
$\Phi = \frac{\mathfrak{A}\sin.m\Phi}{m} - \frac{\mathfrak{B}\sin.(1-m)\Phi}{1-m} + \frac{\mathfrak{C}\sin.(1+m)\Phi}{1+m} - \frac{\mathfrak{D}\sin.(2-m)\Phi}{2-m} +$ etc.
ita vt sit:
$\mathfrak{A} = \frac{(1-m)^2}{1(1-2m)}\cdot\frac{(1+m)^2}{3(1+2m)}\cdot\frac{(2-m)^2}{3(3-2m)}\cdot\frac{(2+m)^2}{5(3+2m)}\cdot$ etc. [?]
$\frac{\mathfrak{B}}{\mathfrak{A}} = \ldots$ etc. [?]
$\frac{\mathfrak{C}}{\mathfrak{B}} = \ldots$ etc. [?]
$\frac{\mathfrak{D}}{\mathfrak{C}} = \ldots$ etc. [?]
$\frac{\mathfrak{E}}{\mathfrak{D}} = \ldots$ etc. [?]
etc.
At

179
Atque ex superiori reductione reperitur
$\mathfrak{A} = \frac{\int x^{m-1}dx(1-x)^{-m}}{m\int x^m dx(1-x)^{m-1}\cdot\int x^{m-1}dx(1-x)^{1-m}}$ [?];
tum vero pro reliquis colligitur ex ipsa forma productorum:
$\frac{\mathfrak{B}}{\mathfrak{A}} = \frac{m}{1-m};\ \frac{\mathfrak{C}}{\mathfrak{B}} = \frac{1-m}{1+m};\ \frac{\mathfrak{D}}{\mathfrak{C}} = \frac{1+m}{2-m};\ \frac{\mathfrak{E}}{\mathfrak{D}} = \frac{2-m}{2+m};$ etc.
ita vt sit
$\mathfrak{B} = \frac{m}{1-m}\mathfrak{A};\ \mathfrak{C} = \frac{m}{1+m}\mathfrak{A};\ \mathfrak{D} = \frac{m}{2-m}\mathfrak{A};\ \mathfrak{E} = \frac{m}{2+m}\mathfrak{A};$ etc.
Ponamus ergo breuitatis gratia
$\int x^m dx(1-x)^{m-1}\cdot\frac{\int x^{m-1}dx(1-x)^{1-m}}{\int x^{m-1}dx(1-x)^{-m}} = M$ [?]
eritque vt sequitur:
$M\Phi = \frac{\sin.m\Phi}{m^2} - \frac{\sin.(1-m)\Phi}{(1-m)^2} + \frac{\sin.(1+m)\Phi}{(1+m)^2} - \frac{\sin.(2-m)\Phi}{(2-m)^2} + \frac{\sin.(2+m)\Phi}{(2+m)^2} -$ etc.
vnde differentiando concludimus fore
$M = \frac{\cos.m\Phi}{m} - \frac{\cos.(1-m)\Phi}{1-m} + \frac{\cos.(1+m)\Phi}{1+m} - \frac{\cos.(2-m)\Phi}{2-m} + \frac{\cos.(2+m)\Phi}{2+m} -$ etc.
quae series ob insignem simplicitatem imprimis est notatu digna: quandoquidem inde, ponendo $\Phi = 0$, deducimus
$M = \frac{1}{m} - \frac{1}{1-m} + \frac{1}{1+m} - \frac{1}{2-m} + \frac{1}{2+m} - \frac{1}{3-m} + \frac{1}{3+m} -$ etc.
cuius seriei summam iam olim ostendi esse
$M = \frac{\pi\cos.m\pi}{\sin.m\pi},$
vnde colligimus hanc elegantem comparationem:
$\int x^m dx(1-x)^{m-1} = \frac{\pi\cos.m\pi}{\sin.m\pi}\cdot\frac{\int x^{m-1}dx(1-x)^{-m}}{\int x^{m-1}dx(1-x)^{1-m}}$ [?]
